content:
An article from Bloomberg reports that Apple Glasses may not feature photo or video recording capabilities at launch. It's said that Apple is considering this approach to address privacy concerns.

However, while I absolutely understand why Apple might consider this option, my personal experience using Ray-Ban Meta smart glasses tells me that video recording is absolutely a core feature that this type of product cannot do without...

Privacy is an important consideration in many of Apple's decisions, and is one of the selling points of its ecosystem.

For example, when it comes to AI features, Apple is committed to keeping as much computation on-device as possible. When cloud computing is needed, its Private Cloud Compute design is intended to ensure that Apple cannot access user data, and to allow security researchers to verify this themselves. This is undoubtedly a good thing.

Privacy concerns with smart glasses

Undoubtedly, smart glasses equipped with video recording capabilities do raise privacy concerns. This was one of the main reasons for the failure of Google Glass back in the day, and users were even saddled with the embarrassing label of being called "Glassholes".

Ray-Ban Meta smart glasses have also sparked privacy controversies, partly because some YouTubers abused the product in truly despicable ways, as reported by BBC News earlier this year.

The company has also faced criticism for being found to have sent sensitive video clips (including accidentally recorded content) to human data annotators.

For all these reasons, I completely understand why Apple would have reservations about adding video recording capabilities to Apple Glasses.

But video recording is indispensable

The problem is that video recording is the key selling point of today's smart glasses, and based on my personal experience, I wouldn't even consider wearing them without this feature.

Let's first list out the various features of Ray-Ban Meta, then share my experience of using each one:

  • Ask Meta AI about what you're seeing
  • Play music
  • Make and receive hands-free voice calls
  • Receive voice notifications, including reading out received messages
  • Press a button or use voice commands to take first-person perspective photos
  • Press a button or use voice commands to capture first-person perspective videos

Ask AI questions

Meta lists this as one of the main selling points of buying the glasses, and without a doubt, it does make a strong first impression. For example, you can look at a famous landmark and have the glasses tell you about it. It can also recognise all sorts of things, from flowers to sculptures. It feels like having Apple Intelligence available anytime, anywhere, without having to take your iPhone out of your pocket.

When I first bought the glasses, I tested these features extensively and was full of anticipation for their future potential applications. I imagined being able to look around at different restaurants and have the glasses tell me the average TripAdvisor rating for each one, as well as what dishes previous customers had recommended.

However, as things stand now, I've barely used this feature, and I would absolutely not consider it a sufficient reason to wear smart glasses on a daily basis.

Playing music

Not a chance: with miniature speakers mounted on the arms, the sound quality simply isn't up to scratch. Headphones will always be a better option, and in-ear headphones are just as convenient.

Hands-free voice calls

Being able to occasionally take a short call while cycling is indeed useful, because I don't want to wear in-ear headphones that block out ambient sound. However, for calls longer than a few sentences, I prefer to stop and deal with them, so this is also not enough of a reason to wear smart glasses on a daily basis.

Voice notifications

This is a feature I do genuinely like. Whether it's iMessage or WhatsApp texts, I can have the glasses read out the message content while I keep walking or cycling. However, again, this benefit alone is not enough to justify the purchase.

Photos and videos

Let's be honest, this is the biggest advantage of current smart glasses. Being able to capture first-person perspective videos without having to use your phone is a fantastic experience, whether it's for special occasions like riding roller coasters or sailing, or for capturing holiday and weekend city sightseeing moments. As I mentioned in my original Ray-Ban Meta smart glasses review:

I've also found this to be a good way to record my cycling journeys. Since I usually wear sunglasses when cycling, simply pressing a button on the arm is much easier than mounting a camera on the bike. My motorcycle enthusiast friends also use their smart glasses in the same way.

This is my biggest motivation for wearing smart glasses, and frankly, I wouldn't consider wearing them at all without this feature. In my opinion, an Apple Glasses product without photo and video capabilities would be dead on arrival before it even launches. (The situation is different for smart glasses with displays; I'll share my experience with those in a separate article, but that's not what we're expecting from the first generation of Apple Glasses.)

What should Apple do?

Fortunately, I believe that striking a balance between practicality and privacy is not impossible.

One of the criticisms levelled at Ray-Ban Meta smart glasses is that although the frames are fitted with a flashing LED to indicate when video is being recorded, the indicator is not visible in bright sunlight. Apple could ensure that its LED indicator is highly visible.

Top Liked Comment from S3xyEV 00

Let's face it.

This species is beyond hope.

AI girlfriends. Cutting in line. Violence sparked by fairy tales. Perversion. Overlooked and quietly swept aside sexual assault cases. A bona fide sadist sitting in the Oval Office.

All I want is a pair of glasses with a screen for translation and subtitles. Navigation prompts would be even better. But unless we stop having hysterical meltdowns over the word "equality", none of it is going to happen.

Technology is inevitably going to be held back as a result.

(If you downvoted this comment, go look in the mirror. You are exactly why we can't have nice things.)

The company could also add external speakers on the arms that play audible cues when recording starts and stops, to alert people nearby. Another option would be to remove the physical buttons for photos and videos, and force users to use voice commands instead. Both of these approaches would make it clear to those around that recording is taking place.

Of course, there's no perfect solution here. There will always be someone who starts recording from a distance and then approaches their target. However, I do believe that combining several of the privacy safeguards mentioned above would work in most situations.

The standard Apple needs to meet is not to be flawless, but to make the device difficult to abuse, so that those with ill intent won't choose it as a tool for their misdeeds.

What are your thoughts on this dilemma? Feel free to share your opinions in the comments section.
